meta.name: Normative knowledge graph for cross-border health-data transfers
meta.scope: The 15 catalogue requirements (reference/requirements.json) for GDPR and the HIPAA Privacy Rule, the alternative routes and conditions the statutes attach to them, and the Irish provisions that supply the GDPR's references to Member State law. Rationale and design decisions: KNOWLEDGE_GRAPH.md.

requirement_roles.applicability: Decides whether a regime applies at all; every other requirement of that regime is gated by it. 'unmet' means the regime does not apply, never a violation.
requirement_roles.obligation: Something that must hold for the transfer under an applicable regime.
requirement_roles.national: A Member State provision that supplies a GDPR reference to national law (an opening). Reached only through implemented_by.

condition_kinds.scope: A factual classification that decides whether a requirement or condition arises, or whether an exception displaces it. Never reported as unmet.
condition_kinds.substantive: Something that must be true or in place; can be unmet.

derived_facts.data_moves_from_eea_to_non_eea_country: Computed by agents.derive_facts from the request and reference/countries.json

units.transfer: Owed for each transfer or disclosure and assessed on the one described (the default when a requirement declares no unit).
units.activity: Owed once for the processing activity, or by the regulated entity, that a transfer belongs to. A single transfer within an existing activity relies on it rather than re-establishing it; the unit's basis quotes the text that attaches it to the activity.

correspondences.note: Both act on another's behalf under a required contract (Art. 28(3); 164.504(e)). Not interchangeable: a business associate can be a GDPR controller for its own purposes, and a covered entity can be a business associate.

Different tests: Recital 26 asks whether anyone is reasonably likely to identify the person; 164.514(b) accepts expert determination or safe-harbour removal of identifiers. Meeting the HIPAA standard does not by itself make data anonymous under the GDPR.

Both reduce identifiability yet stay regulated: pseudonymised data remain personal data (Recital 26) and a limited data set remains PHI. Their identifier rules differ, so one does not imply the other.
Both are the individual's permission, with different validity rules (Arts. 4(11), 7 and 9(2)(a); 164.508(c) core elements). One does not satisfy the other.

Overlapping but distinct scopes: GDPR health data is any personal data revealing health status, whoever holds it; PHI is individually identifiable health information held by a covered entity or business associate.
